div.div:
What is being communicated?
- Bulk data (DMA transfers)
- Memory-mapped transactions
- Interrupts (MSI/MSI-X)
No "commands" like I2C;
it's a transaction-based memory access

- PCIe is Lane-based
- A PCIe link consists of multiple lanes:
- x1 -> 1 lane
- x4 -> 4 lanes
- x16 -> 16 lanes
- Each lane has a set of TX/RX (full duplex)

div.div:
Root Complex
- commonly owned by a CPU
- forwards packets based on address/ID routing (same as switches)
- routing is hop-by-hop;
the root complex only forwards like a bridge, not a global path planner

div.div:
High bandwidth demand
Example: streaming a large dataset
like
- AI model loading
- reading a large video file
With PCIe
- SSD → Memory uses DMA over PCIe
- High lane bandwidth (x4/x16)
Without PCIe
- I2C/SPI → completely infeasible

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 274px; height: 1px; padding-top: 525px; margin-left: 956px;

div.div:
Latency matters
Example: sending commands to a high-performance accelerator
like
- CPU memory writing a command to GPU register
- CPU memory writing NVMe commands to SSD submission queue (in RAM or BAR)
With PCIe
- Much lower latency than slow buses
- Still flexible (packet-based)
Without PCIe
- Ethernet → too much overhead
- I2C → too slow

div.div:
Memory semantics needed (wanting to treat device like memory)
Example
- CPU memory writing NVMe commands to SSD submission queue, which locates in RAM or BAR
With PCIe
- Device exposes BAR (memory-mapped region)
- CPU just does:
write(address)
read(address)

div.div:
CPU should not move data (DMA)
Example: Network packet reception
- NIC receives packets from network
- Writes directly into system memory
With PCIe
- NIC performs:
Memory Write → Ram
- CPU only processes after
Without PCIe-style DMA
- CPU would copy byte-by-byte → wasteful

div.div:
Scalability needed
Example: Expanding a system with multiple accelerators
With PCIe
- Add switches
- Fan out links
- Each gets dedicated bandwidth

Isolation matters
Example: Faulty device shouldn't break others
With PCIe
- Point-to-point links
- Switch isolates downstream subtree
Without PCIe
- I2C → one bad device can pull the whole bus down

div.div:
Complexity is acceptable
Example: High-performance compute node design
- When system is performance-critical
- Engineers accept:
- complex routing
- driver stack
- enumeration
With PCIe
- Trade complexity for performance

div.div:
Control-oriented communication
Example: Fan control
like
- Command: "set PWM = 60%"
Why not PCIe
- You don't need:
- DMA
- memory-mapped queues
- high throughput
Better choice
- I2C / GPIO / PMBus

box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;

div.div:
Low bandwidth / small data
Tiny and infrequent.
Example: temperature sensors read a few bytes every second
Why not PCIe
- Massive overkill:
- SerDes PHY
- lane routing
- protocol stack
Better choice
- I2C / SMBus

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 274px; height: 1px; padding-top: 745px; margin-left: 1606px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;

div.div:
Hard real-time / deterministic timing
Example: Precise motor control loop
- Needs exact timing guarantees
Why not PCIe
- Packet-based
- Variable latency (small, yes, but not deterministic)
- Arbitration + buffering
Better choice
- SPI / dedicated real-time bus / direct wiring

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 274px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1045px; margin-left: 1606px;

div.div:
Power / cost constrained systems
Cost / power matters more than performance
Example: embedded IoT device
- Battery-power
- Simple MCU
Like:
- Smart temperature + humidity sensor node:
- typical setup:
- small MCU chip
- Sensors: temperature, humidity
- Communication: WiFi / BLE
- Power: battery (months → years
- What it does:
- wakes up every few seconds/minutes
- reads a few bytes from sensor
- send a small packet
- go back to sleep
Why not PCIe
- High power PHY
- Complex PCB routing
- Expensive silicon
Better choice
- I2C / SPI / UART

div.div:
When memory semantics are NOT useful
Example: event-driven messaging
- "notify me when X happens"
Why not PCIe
- PCIe is:
- memory-access-centric
- Messaging is:
- event-centric
Better choice
- Message-based protocols (CAN, Ethernet, etc)

Example: one MCU + one peripheral
- Fixed topology
- No expansion
Why not PCIe
- PCIe shines when:
- multiple devices
- expansion
- switching
Better choice
- SPI / direct bus
Without PCIe
- I2C → one bad device can pull the whole bus down

Example: Communication across machines
Why not PCIe
- Short-ranged (board-level)
- Not designed for long cables / routing across systems
Better choice
- Ethernet / network protocols

div.div:
Signal Integrity
- PCIe is high-speed serial
- Signals degrade over:
- long PCB traces
- connectors
- vias / impedance mismatch
Results:
- Limited trace length
- Need:
- retimers / redrivers
Hence:
- CPU ↔ slot is short
- Long cables are rare/expensive

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 214px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1405px; margin-left: 4546px;

div.div:
Lane count is physically limited
- Each lane = 2 differential pairs (TX/RX)
- CPU/package has finite pins
Results:
- Can't just "add more PCIe"
- Typical:
- Desktop CPI: ~16-24 lanes
- Server CPU: ~64-128 lanes
Tradeoff:
- GPU vs SSD vs NIC → resource contention

div.div:
Power + heat constraints
- High speed = high switching = heat
Results:
- PCIe Gen5/Gen6:
- serious thermal issues
- need better materials, cooling
Hence:
- Not everything uses PCIe even if "faster"

div.div:
Latency floor
Physics + protocol
Even if fast:
- Serialization/deserialization (SerDes)
- Packetization
- Switch hops
Results:
- PCIe is NOT zero latency
- Typically:
- hundreds of nanoseconds to microseconds
Hence:
- Some things use SPI, not PCIe

div.div:
Not deterministic
- PCIe is:
- packet-based
- shared fabric
Results:
- Timing is not predictable
Hence:
- Not for:
- hard real-time control
- precise timing loops
- Use instead:
- SPI / I2C / dedicated signals

div.div:
No implicit broadcast / simple sharing
- PCIe is:
- point-to-point + routed
Results:
- No simple "everyone hears this" bus
Hence:
- You must:
- Explicitly route
- Configure topology

Complex initialization
Not plug-and-go simple
- PCIe requires:
- enumeration
- BAR assignment
- link training
Results:
- Needs:
- firmware + OS cooperation
- Not usable in
- ultra-minimal systems

Requires a root complex
CPU-centric
- Everything anchored at root complex (CPU)
Results:
- Devices don't form arbitrary networks easily
- Even peer-to-peer is still constrained by topology + permissions

Inefficient for small/simple tasks
- PCIe overhead:
- packets
- headers
- transactions
Results:
- Bad for:
- toggling a pin
- reading 1 byte occasionally
- Better:
- I2C / PCI / GPIO

Oversubscription
Hidden bottleneck
Example:
- 4 NVMe drives on a switch
- uplink = x4

Results:
- Looks fast, but real throughput collapses under load

- Tree structure (root → switch → endpoints)

- Placement matters
- Not all devices communicates equally well

Cost / complexity
PCIe requires:
- complex controllers
- PHY (SerDes)
- strict layout rules
Results:
- Expensive silicon + PCB

div.div:
What must exist before PCIe even starts:
- Power rails stable (slot / device / PHY)
- Reference clock present (100 MHz common refclk or SRIS)
- Reset signals correct (PERST# released at right time)
Ownership:
- Board design + power sequencing + sometimes BMC/GPIO
Dependencies:
- VRMs
- clock generators
- Reset tree (CPLD / PCH / CPU)

switch.text: What must exist before PCIe even starts:...

div.div:
This is where PCIe becomes alive.
Core concept:
Devices run the LTSSM (Link Training and Status State Machine):
- Detect -> Polling -> Configuration -> L0
What happens:
- Lane detection
- Speed negotiation (Gen1 -> Gen5...)
- Width negotiation (x1/x4/x8/x16)
- Equalization (high-speed tuning)
Ownership:
- Hardware (PHY + controller)

switch.text: This is where PCIe becomes alive....

div.div:
Enumeration = turning a physical device into a usable software object
What happens:
- Root Complex scans bus
- Assigns:
- Bus numbers
- BARs (memory regions)
- IRQs
- Loads drivers
Ownership:
- Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) -> early
- OS (Linux kernel) -> runtime
Dependencies:
- Device tree (on ARM/BMC systems)
- ACPI (on x86)
- Kernel drivers

What happens:
- Memory transactions (MMIO)
- DMA transfers
- Interrupts (MSI/MSI-X)
Ownership:
- Device driver
- Device firmware
- Application layer (indirectly)
Dependencies:
- Memory coherency
- IOMMU (if enabled)
- Driver correctness

PCIe is not "fail once and die" -- it tries to recover
Mechanisms:
- AER (Advanced Error Reporting)
- Link retraining
- Function reset (FLR)
- Hot reset
Ownership:
- Hardware + OS + driver cooperation

- TX sends small detection signals
- RX checks:
Do I see termination on the other side?
If yes → move on
If no → stay here

- RX: tunes until maxed out

- Tries to recognize patterns

RX cleans up what remains:
- CTLE (analog) → boosts high frequencies
- DFE (digital) → subtracts influence of previous bits (undo ISI)
DFE: "I know what I decided the previous bit was
→ I subtract its expected residue from the current sample"

div.div:
1. Each lane is received independently
via RX + CDR
2. Data goes into per-lane elastic buffer
3. The system detects SKP on each lane and selects a set within the same window, then shifts buffers to align them
4. Then it outputs them as a synchronized group

- During bring-up: Training sequences TS1 / TS2
- During normal operation: SKP ordered sets
SKP: checkpoint

div.div:
Sequence Numbering
- Every outgoing packet (TLP) gets tagged with a sequence number
- Lets the receiver detect:
- Missing packets
- Duplicates
- Out-of-order arrivals

div.div:
ACK/NAK handling
- Receiver sends:
- ACK
- NACK
- Transmitted packets are stored in a replay buffer
- If a NAK is received:
- DLL retransmits from buffer

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 214px; height: 1px; padding-top: 5225px; margin-left: 3467px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;

div.div:
CRC / integrity check (LCRC)
- Each packet carries a Link CRC
- Receiver:
- Computes CRC
- Compares → detect corruption
If mismatch → triggers NAK → replay

div.div:
Flow control
- Prevents overrunning the receiver
Receiver says:
"I have X buffer space"
Sender:
"I will only send within that limit"

div.div:
Reference clock (refclk)
- Low-frequency, stable clock (e.g., 100MHz)
- Used for:
- PLL input
- LTSSM timing
- General digital logic
May be:
- Shared between devices (common clock)
- Independent per device (separate clock)

Recovered clock (data clock)
- Extracted from incoming bitstream
- Used to:
- Sample incoming serial data
- Drive RX logic timing
